explain.say: On 11 February 1990, Nelson Mandela walked out of prison near Cape Town, his fist raised, after 27 years behind bars. Four years later he was elected president in South Africa's first election open to all adults. Look at the timeline. How did a system built to last for ever fall within a few years?

events.label: Soweto
events.ask: What happened at Sharpeville and Soweto?

explain.say: Apartheid means separateness in Afrikaans. From 1948 the law classified everyone by race, controlled where Black people could live and work with pass laws, and kept the vote for white people. Look at the sizes: around 1950 Black South Africans were about two thirds of the people, but laws reserved only about 13 percent of the land for them. What would that do to families?

Now the map. At Sharpeville in March 1960 police shot dead 69 people protesting the pass laws. On 16 June 1976 in Soweto, schoolchildren marched against being taught in Afrikaans; police opened fire, and the photo of 12-year-old Hector Pieterson went round the world. Hundreds died in the uprising. We remember them. How might these events have changed world opinion?

Why did it end? See the causes. Strikes, boycotts and township protests made the country hard to govern. Sanctions and sports boycotts isolated it, the economy struggled, and when the Cold War ended in 1989 the government lost its claim to be fighting communism. President F. W. de Klerk unbanned the ANC in 1990 and negotiated with Mandela. Which pressure mattered most?

explain.say: Was it a miracle? See both views. A peaceful vote in 1994, a new constitution, and Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission; yet about 14,000 people died in political violence from 1990 to 1994, and deep inequality remains. Thank you for thinking so carefully. Exam tip: separate political change from economic change.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: A political revolution; social change slower.

faq.a: A system of racial segregation and white minority rule in South Africa from 1948 to the early 1990s. Laws classified people by race, restricted where Black, Coloured and Indian South Africans could live and work, controlled movement with passes and denied them the vote.

Mass resistance inside South Africa, international sanctions and isolation, economic decline, the end of the Cold War and negotiations between Nelson Mandela and President F. W. de Klerk led to the end of apartheid laws and the first democratic election in April 1994.
asks: Who was F. W. de Klerk?

faq.q: What was the Truth and Reconciliation Commission?
faq.a: A body chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu from 1996 that heard testimony from victims and perpetrators of apartheid-era abuses. Perpetrators who fully disclosed politically motivated crimes could apply for amnesty, which some victims' families found painful.

faq.q: What happened at Sharpeville and Soweto?
faq.a: At Sharpeville on 21 March 1960 police killed 69 people protesting pass laws. In Soweto on 16 June 1976 police fired on students marching against Afrikaans-language teaching, starting an uprising in which hundreds died. Both events drew world condemnation.

faq.q: How much land did Black South Africans have under the land laws?
faq.a: The 1913 Natives Land Act and the 1936 Native Trust and Land Act reserved only about 7 and then about 13 percent of the land for Black South Africans, who were around two thirds of the population.
asks: What was the Natives Land Act?

facts: The National Party came to power in South Africa in 1948.
Nelson Mandela was released on 11 February 1990.
South Africa's first democratic election was held on 27 April 1994.

quiz.say: Mandela was imprisoned from 1962 to 1990. How many years is that?
quiz.why: 1990 minus 1962 is 28 calendar years; he served about 27 full years.

quiz.say: Who chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission?
quiz.why: Archbishop Desmond Tutu chaired the commission from 1996.

wrong.1: De Klerk was the president who negotiated the transition.
wrong.2: Hector Pieterson was a schoolboy killed in Soweto in 1976.
